First off: I have much respect for what the Voat team and community is trying to build here. But sadly, this week has proven to me something that I have suspected ever since the NSA leaks, but couldn't ever bring myself to admit.

I'm a free speech absolutist. I do find content like FPH, Stormfront, and the jailbait subverses to be personally abhorrent, and I will defend the right of private site operators to limit what can be displayed on their own sites. But I will also defend the right of private citizens to start their own communities and enjoy their right to free speech, no matter how offensive I may find it.

This week has finally made it clear to me that free speech on the Internet is dead. The structure of the Internet ensures that sufficiently motivated and funded adversaries can effectively shut you down if they want to, regardless of such quaint notions as "rights" and "laws." The Internet was a great idea, but it's been captured by the powers that be, and it's now effectively broken.

So why can't we seem to fix it? Well, what makes this problem impossible to fix is that it isn't just the Internet that's broken.

First of all, there is a war on general purpose computing, and the side of control has almost completely won. Nobody really "owns" their own box now, even F/OSS zealots, thanks to endless layers of complex, often proprietary software and firmware (with convenient backdoors and vulnerabilities for governments to exploit). Even if you somehow get a secure server up, the multitude of gatekeepers -- from ISPs to hosting providers to merchant gateways and on and on -- can effectively exercise "hard" control of your speech if they need to shut you down. "Soft" control is also possible using social manipulation techniques such as those employed by JTRIG and GHCQ. It's too much for anyone but well-equipped nation-states to fight against, and even they have trouble dealing with the problem.

Well, I give up. The Internet as we know it is fucked. Hell, computing as we know it is fucked. The only hope lies with the projects trying to build a constellation of truly free systems based on decentralization. Who knows what it will look like, but I'm sure it will take inspiration from the following...

  • Self-manufactured systems (using 3D printers and/or easily verifiable components)
  • Mesh networks that don't rely on centralized concepts such as domain names and ISPs
  • Distributed storage of controversial content, such as that provided by Freenet or some sort of blockchain-type system
  • Virtual, anonymous currencies
  • Strong cryptography
  • Concealment of origin for "controversial" communications
  • High deniability such as that provided by Truecrypt
  • Resilience and the ability to fall back to "sneakernet" type solutions if required

This type of computing will be inconvenient, and it will never be widely adopted. However, those of us who enjoy discussing controversial ideas without being tracked and manipulated will gladly embrace these solutions once they become usable.

From now on, I'm putting my effort and funding into these types of projects. We have to start on this now while the tools are available.

Good luck, Voaters, and so long. May you succeed against the odds.
